_note: AI reader 57's anchors (opioids with sedatives and alcohol, cocaine with alcohol, lower tolerance after a break); second reader AI reader 61.

tasks.locator: Results > Overdose Deaths, 2nd paragraph (p. 89); Dose-Dependent Overdose Risk, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 90)
tasks.extracted: Of 2,182,374 North Carolina residents dispensed an opioid analgesic in 2010, 478 died of an overdose involving one (0.022%), within 629 such deaths in all; there were 2,181,847 person-years of opioid analgesic exposure. A benzodiazepine had been dispensed in the past year to 80.0% (1,747,166) of opioid analgesic recipients. Overdose death rates were about ten times higher with benzodiazepines and opioids concurrently (7.0 per 10,000 person-years, 95% CI 6.3, 7.8) than with opioid analgesics only (0.7, CI 0.6, 0.9); against patients on the same opioid dose, the rate difference was 2.8 per 10,000 person-years in the lowest dose group and 45.8 in the highest. Editors' calculation: if 80% of the 2,181,847 person-years were exposed to benzodiazepines, 7.0 per 10,000 person-years would mean over 1,200 deaths, more than the 478 among patients or the 629 in all; the paper does not say how benzodiazepine exposure was timed in the rates, and no covariate is used.

tasks.locator: Methods > Exposure Definition, last sentence (p. 88); Statistical Analysis, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (p. 89); Discussion, 11th and 12th paragraphs (p. 94)
tasks.extracted: Benzodiazepine exposure was set for each person as any dispensing in the 365 days before death or the end of the study. Incidence rates and rate ratios came from Poisson regression with person-days at risk as the offset and generalized estimating equations; no covariate was used. The authors name as the greatest limitation of the study that patients at higher doses are likely to have more serious illness, say no additional covariate information was available to adjust for the likelihood of treatment, and say data on other confounders were not controlled for.

tasks.locator: Methods > Outcome Definition (p. 88); Results > Overdose Deaths, 1st paragraph (p. 89) and 3rd paragraph (p. 90); Dose-Dependent Overdose Risk, 2nd paragraph (p. 90)
tasks.extracted: North Carolina residents who died in 2010 of an unintentional or undetermined drug overdose were included if at least one of eight opioid analgesics was judged by the medical examiner to play a primary or additive role; the role of each drug was judged by the examiners' toxicologists from the scene investigation, toxicology, available medical records and interviews. There were 629 such deaths. Benzodiazepines were judged involved by medical examiners in 61.4% (386) of them. Among the 629 deaths, 24.0% (151) had no opioid analgesic dispensed in the 365 days before death. Editors' calculation: 386 of 629 is 61.4%; national certificates named benzodiazepines in 26.2% of all opioid overdose deaths in 2010 (Tori et al.).

tasks.locator: Methods > Outcome Definition (p. 88); Discussion, 9th paragraph (p. 94)
tasks.extracted: Deaths were counted only where an opioid analgesic was judged to have a primary or additive role, not where it was merely present; records were abstracted for decedents with toxicology results, 824 (92%) of the deaths identified. The authors say medical examiner determination of death inherently contains an element of subjective clinical judgment, that people may have obtained opioid analgesics from other states or outside medical channels, and that all studies relying on medical examiner or vital statistics data are limited in ascribing causality for the involvement of drug substances. Editors' note: this is one state in one year, and the count says how often examiners judged a benzodiazepine involved, not how much it added to the risk of dying.

tasks.locator: Methods > Data Sources and Study Population, 2nd paragraph (p. 494); Results, 7th paragraph (begins p. 495, figures on p. 497); Figure 3 (p. 500)
tasks.extracted: In the US national death-certificate file (National Vital Statistics System multiple cause of death), 2004–2011, benzodiazepine involvement in opioid analgesic overdose deaths rose from 18.4% of deaths in 2004 to 31% in 2011 (p-trend < 0.0001), and opioid involvement in benzodiazepine overdose deaths from 69% in 2004 to 75% in 2011 (p-trend = 0.0017). Overdose deaths were those with an underlying cause of drug poisoning; an opioid analgesic was a contributing cause coded T40.2 to T40.4 and a benzodiazepine one coded T42.4.

tasks.locator: Limitations, 1st paragraph (p. 500)
tasks.extracted: The authors state that approximately 25% of drug overdose death certificates do not specify the drugs involved, owing to lack of toxicologic testing or failure to record results, so the number and rate of deaths are likely underestimates, and that population-based denominators do not account for differences in drug use across groups or over time. Editors' note: this series draws on the same national certificate source as the 1999–2017 series in the first anchor, so it does not count as an independent source.

tasks.locator: Results > Overdose Deaths, 1st paragraph (p. 89)
tasks.extracted: In North Carolina in 2010, 629 deaths involved an opioid analgesic in a primary or additive role, as judged by medical examiners. Ethanol was involved in 12.2% (77) of them; heroin was present in 1.3% (8) and cocaine in 8.4% (53). Editors' note: one state in one year, among deaths involving an opioid painkiller and judged by medical examiners, so this is not a like-for-like test of whether certificates under-record alcohol.

tasks.locator: Main text, 2nd paragraph (p. 1060); 3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 1061)
tasks.extracted: A For Debate paper that presents no new data. From studies it cites without sample sizes or years: alcohol is the most commonly detected substance in heroin-related deaths (about 50%) and is detected in approximately a third of methadone-related deaths; several studies of heroin deaths report an inverse relation between blood alcohol and blood morphine at post mortem, with blood morphine 60% lower where blood alcohol was above 100 mg/dl than below it (United States and Australia). The authors give as the prevailing interpretation additive or interactive effects on breathing, and list other routes to the same findings: alcohol may impair judgement of tolerance, alcohol use is linked with heroin relapse, people reducing heroin may drink more so that falling tolerance could be the underlying problem, and polydrug use may mark people at risk for other reasons. They say the effect of alcohol with heroin on breathing at realistic levels of drinking has not been evaluated systematically and that a pharmacodynamic or pharmacokinetic interaction remains unproven. Editors' note: the post-mortem limit that White and Irvine state is not mentioned in this paper.

tasks.locator: Factors determining susceptibility to opioid overdose > Metabolic factors, paragraph beginning 'It is also important to recognize' (p. 965); Opioid-drug interactions > Sedatives, 1st to 3rd paragraphs (pp. 968-969)
tasks.extracted: A narrative review. It says there is considerable evidence that many overdoses are due to the combined effects of opioids with other drugs, chiefly alcohol and benzodiazepines, but cites no source in that sentence and describes no study of alcohol with an opioid in people. It reasons from receptor pharmacology: alcohol and benzodiazepines are relatively weak breathing depressants on their own; alcohol acts at the GABA-A receptor complex, at a site other than the benzodiazepine site, and blocks NMDA receptors, effects that the review says should be at least additive with those of mu-receptor opioids. It advises that post-mortem drug measurements be treated with caution because levels vary with time after death, tissue sampled and body site, and post-mortem metabolism is possible.

tasks.locator: Methods and Findings, 5th paragraph (p. 1); Figure (p. 3)
tasks.extracted: Recent pregabalin (a prescription in the previous 120 days): 69 of 1,417 people who died of an opioid-related cause (4.9%) and 153 of 5,097 matched controls (3.0%); unadjusted OR 1.85 (95% CI 1.36–2.53), adjusted OR 1.68 (1.19–2.36), adjusted for gabapentin, antidepressants, benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants, number of medications, Charlson score, number of prescribers and pharmacies, long-acting opioid and opioid dose. Prescription overlapping the index date: 60 (4.2%) against 121 (2.4%), adjusted OR 1.81 (1.26–2.60). Controls matched on use of other CNS depressants (1,199 cases, 3,935 controls): 59 (4.9%) against 116 (3.0%), adjusted OR 2.00 (1.39–2.88).

tasks.locator: Methods and Findings, 3rd and 5th paragraphs (p. 1); Figure (p. 3)
tasks.extracted: Dose analysis by prescribed daily dose (the study's strata), against no recent pregabalin: low or moderate (up to 300 mg a day) 52 cases (3.7%) and 128 controls (2.5%), adjusted OR 1.52 (1.04–2.22); high (above 300 mg a day) 17 (1.2%) and 25 (0.5%), adjusted OR 2.51 (1.24–5.06); no test of a trend is reported. Predefined comparison exposure, NSAIDs: 531 cases and 1,830 controls (35.9%), adjusted OR 1.04 (0.90–1.19). Editors' note: 531 of 1,417 cases is 37.5%, not the 34.5% printed in the Figure.

tasks.locator: Methods and Findings, 1st to 4th paragraphs (p. 1); Table (p. 2)
tasks.extracted: A population-based nested case–control study of Ontario residents eligible for public drug coverage who received prescription opioids between 1 August 1997 and 31 December 2016; the methods, data sources and analyses follow the authors' earlier gabapentin study, with differences described. Cases died of an opioid-related cause, excluding suicide and homicide; each was matched to up to 4 controls on age (within 3 years), sex, index year, history of chronic kidney disease and Charlson score, and conditional logistic regression was adjusted for characteristics still imbalanced after matching. After matching, cases were more likely than controls to have recent benzodiazepines (1,073, 75.7% against 2,735, 53.7%; standardized difference 0.45 against weighted controls), other CNS depressants (35.4% against 23.8%), long-acting opioids (51.4% against 36.3%) and opioid doses of 200 or more morphine milligram equivalents a day (27.0% against 16.2%); 43.0% of cases and 43.1% of controls were in the lowest income fifth. Editors' note: the letter does not say how opioid-related deaths were identified, and it has no limitations section.

tasks.locator: Discussion, single paragraph (p. 1); Grant Support (p. 2)
tasks.extracted: The authors read the result as compelling evidence for a potentially life-threatening drug-drug interaction between pregabalin and opioids, similar to that seen with gabapentin, note that more than half of Ontario residents starting pregabalin are also prescribed an opioid, and call for a revision of the pregabalin product monographs. The work was funded by the Ontario Ministry of Health and Long-Term Care. Editors' note: this reading is causal and goes beyond an adjusted odds ratio of 1.68 from dispensing records; the letter gives no reason for pregabalin prescribing.

tasks.locator: Methods and Materials > Subjects, 1st paragraph; Procedures, 1st paragraph; Study Design, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Eight non-treatment-seeking volunteers (4 men, 4 women; mean age 33) who were already using cocaine and alcohol together, with cocaine as the preferred drug, and who met DSM-IV criteria for cocaine dependence and alcohol abuse, stayed as inpatients and were told to abstain from drugs and alcohol for 3 days before admission. Double-blind, within-person, three 480-minute sessions in random order, no more often than every 2 days: four doses of intranasal cocaine (1 mg/kg every 30 minutes) with oral alcohol (1 g/kg after the first cocaine dose and 120 mg/kg at 60 minutes, calculated to hold plasma alcohol near 100 mg/dL); the same cocaine with placebo alcohol; lactose in place of cocaine with the same alcohol (no session had both drugs replaced by placebo). Participants knew the three possible conditions; doses were set by lean body weight. The usual intake printed for the group (cocaine 5 g a week with a standard error of 7; 14 standard drinks a week with a standard error of 50) cannot be right for 8 people.

tasks.locator: Results, 1st paragraph (p. 252); Figure 1 and its legend (p. 253)
tasks.extracted: Heart rate was significantly higher after each dose with cocaine plus alcohol than with cocaine alone (p = .002) or alcohol alone (p = .002). Printed areas under the curve over 480 minutes (in the key inside the Figure 1 image, so not in the text layer): 40,289 (SEM 940) for the combination, 35,658 (647) for cocaine alone, 34,778 (933) for alcohol alone. Systolic and diastolic pressure rose with both cocaine conditions, with no significant difference between cocaine plus alcohol and cocaine alone; the combination raised systolic (p = .008) and diastolic (p = .003) pressure above alcohol alone. Read approximately from the figure (an image): the combination peaked near 95 beats per minute at 120 minutes and cocaine alone near 82. Editors' calculation (area divided by 480 minutes): averages of about 83.9, 74.3 and 72.5 beats per minute.

tasks.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (starts p. 252, continues p. 253); Table 1 (p. 255); Discussion, 4th paragraph (starts p. 256; the area ratio is on p. 256)
tasks.extracted: Cocaine: peak 893 (SEM 114) ng/mL at 113 minutes with alcohol against 754 (114) at 116 minutes without (the peak difference is not tested); area under the curve 153,562 (19,489) against 135,371 (19,892) ng x min/mL, described as about 15% greater with alcohol, p = .035; half-life 85 and 83 minutes. Cocaethylene, formed only with the combination: half-life 156 (SEM 15.3) minutes, longer than cocaine (p = .001); peak 114 (18) ng/mL at 180 minutes, about 22% of the cocaine concentration then; area under the curve 31,050 (4,706), 0.20 (0.01) of the cocaine area; ratio to cocaine about 0.13 at 120 minutes and 0.40 at 360 minutes. Editors' calculation from the printed means: the cocaine area is 13.4% greater with alcohol.

tasks.locator: Results, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Figures 2 and 3 (pp. 254-255, images)
tasks.extracted: Rating of any high greater with the combination than with cocaine alone but short of significance (p = .09); the cocaine-high rating did not differ from cocaine alone (and was greater than with alcohol alone, p = .002); feel good greater than with cocaine alone (p = .04), peaking at 120 minutes, with a slight reduction in feel good with cocaine alone over the sessions. Rush, sleepy, paranoid, crash, sad or depressed and desire for cocaine showed no statistically significant findings (no values printed).

tasks.locator: Results, 4th paragraph (continued, p. 253); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (pp. 255-256)
tasks.extracted: Plasma alcohol was lower with the combination than with alcohol alone (p = .008; data not shown in the paper); 90 minutes into the session (30 minutes after the second alcohol dose) it averaged 99 (SE 7) mg/dL with cocaine and 118 (10) without, against a target near 100. The authors suggest that swallowed cocaine slows alcohol absorption by narrowing blood vessels in the stomach.

tasks.locator: Methods and Materials > Data Analysis, 1st paragraph (p. 252); Discussion, 4th paragraph (pp. 256-257) and 5th, 6th, 7th and 9th paragraphs (p. 257)
tasks.extracted: All 15 measures were compared as areas under the curve in a repeated-measures analysis, with planned comparisons of the combination against each drug alone, one comparison per measure; every test with p below .05 (one tailed) was counted as significant, with no correction, justified by directional hypotheses from the authors' earlier study. The authors suggest cocaethylene may matter more for heart effects late in the session (4th paragraph), and say the findings point to an increased risk of organ ischaemia, infarction and arrhythmia (5th); the paper reports no heart events or rhythm findings, and no test separates an effect of cocaethylene from the rise in cocaine. Participants were chosen because they already used both drugs (6th paragraph); the authors say it is unclear whether people who use both drugs have a premorbid vulnerability to psychiatric disorders or whether the combination is more toxic to the central nervous system than cocaine alone (7th); they list the intranasal route as a limit, since smoked or injected cocaine might give larger effects (9th).

tasks.locator: Methods > Inclusion and exclusion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (p. 774); Table 1 (p. 775)
tasks.extracted: The review (a narrative review: databases and years are stated, but no counts of records found or excluded) lists in Table 1 prospective laboratory studies with 6 to 34 people each; the study above is one of them. Cocaine was given intranasally or intravenously and never smoked, and the placebo in most studies was a 4 mg or 5 mg dose of cocaine (Table 1 footnote). Only a few studies had at least two active doses of each drug, which the review says is needed to speak of synergy, so it uses the word 'potentiation' loosely. Editors' count of the Table 1 rows: 14 studies, 13 of them with 12 or fewer people.

tasks.locator: Results > Prospective research > Heart rate, 1st paragraph (p. 774); Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 1st paragraph (p. 776); Cocaethylene production, 1st paragraph (p. 777)
tasks.extracted: As described by the review: when cocaine was given at the same time as or after alcohol, most studies showed a trend towards greater-than-additive heart-rate effects but did not support synergy; blood cocaine was up to 30% higher with the combination in five studies (the study above among them); blood alcohol was unchanged in one study and about 10% lower, not significantly, in four; cocaethylene formed only when both drugs were given, never with either alone (six studies), and also when alcohol followed cocaine by 30 minutes. The review's text and Table 1 describe the study above as showing greater-than-additive increases in heart rate and in 'any high'; that study compared the combination only with each drug alone, had no session with both drugs replaced by placebo, and found any high short of significance (p = .09).

tasks.locator: Results > Prospective research > Heart rate, 2nd paragraph (pp. 774, 776); Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 2nd paragraph (p. 776)
tasks.extracted: Order of dosing: in a 6-person study (Perez-Reyes, 1994) in which cocaine was given 30 minutes before alcohol, heart-rate rises were additive, blood cocaine was not higher than with cocaine alone and the rating of high did not change, unlike earlier studies in which alcohol came first; cocaethylene formed in both orders. The review calls alcohol before cocaine the more common order, without citing a source.

tasks.locator: Retrospective studies > Cocaethylene and toxicity, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (pp. 778-779)
tasks.extracted: As described by the review: whether cocaethylene or the higher cocaine level explains the heart-rate rise is controversial, and talk of greater cardiotoxicity may be premature, since no retrospective study shows unequivocally that the combination leads to more of it; one study of over 1,000 emergency-room toxicology screens found no more cardiovascular problems in people positive for both drugs than for one, and another found less chest pain but more back and limb pain with the combination, without an alcohol-only group. A single case report of an 18-year-old who died suddenly of cardiotoxicity after cocaine, alcohol and cannabis is set against the larger study.

tasks.locator: Results > Prospective research > Effect on perceived inebriation, 1st paragraph (pp. 776-777); Table 1 (p. 775)
tasks.extracted: As described by the review: in several studies cocaine produced a slight decrease in alcohol-induced inebriation (Farre 1993; Higgins 1993; Farre 1997) and in another it had no effect (Perez-Reyes and Jeffcoat 1992); Table 1 labels the Farre studies' falls non-significantly reduced drunk and lists 9, 8, 8 and 11 people in the four studies. Alcohol given before or together with cocaine led to a greater perceived cocaine high or global intoxication in six studies; an EEG index of intoxication rose in step with the high in one; alcohol raised the preference for cocaine over cash in one.

tasks.locator: Results > Prospective research > Behavioural, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: As described by the review: alcohol-induced deficits in the laboratory were consistently lessened by cocaine: digit-symbol substitution (Foltin 1993; Higgins 1993), sedation (Foltin 1993), and learning and psychomotor performance (Higgins 1992).

tasks.locator: Results > Prospective research > Blood levels and toxicokinetics, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: As described by the review: compared with alcohol alone, the combination had no effect on blood alcohol in one study and produced a slight, non-significant decrease (about 10%) in four. The review offers reduced alcohol absorption after cocaine narrows blood vessels as one possible explanation and says cocaethylene is too small to account for the lower alcohol levels.

tasks.locator: Retrospective studies > Operating motor vehicles, 1st paragraph (p. 778); Conclusions, 2nd paragraph (starts p. 780; the driving sentence is on p. 781)
tasks.extracted: As described by the review: retrospective research shows a substantial effect of alcohol alone on driving, and the combination gave no definitive protection from alcohol's impairing effects, since 21 of 600 fatally injured drivers in Los Angeles County and 12 of 285 in Spain tested positive for both drugs; the conclusions say there is no evidence that co-use of cocaine adds to alcohol-induced driving deficits. The abstract's statement that cocaine counters driving deficits has no prospective driving test behind it in the text.

tasks.locator: Methods and Materials > Cocaine Study Drug Administration Sessions, 1st paragraph (pp. 251-252); Results, 2nd, 3rd and 4th paragraphs (pp. 252-253); Discussion, 3rd paragraph (pp. 255-256)
tasks.extracted: The one multiple-dose study read in full reports visual analogue ratings of any high, rush, sleepy, paranoid, sad or depressed, crash, desire for cocaine and feel good, and a quality-of-high scale, but no rating of drunkenness or intoxication; sleepy showed no significant difference between conditions (no values printed), and any high was higher with the combination than with cocaine alone but short of significance (p = .09), although the review counts this study among six with a greater high. Plasma alcohol was lower with cocaine than with alcohol alone (p = .008; 99 against 118 mg/dL 90 minutes into the session).

tasks.locator: Tolerance, paragraphs beginning 'Tolerance could also account for' and 'The loss of tolerance for the different effects'
tasks.extracted: As described by the review: tolerance could account for a relatively high risk after a period of abstinence, because loss of tolerance over time may give a much greater effect at a given dose, so that a dose that once gave euphoria with minimal breathing depression may produce pronounced respiratory impairment. It cites one study (Tagliaro and colleagues, 1998) that found less morphine in the hair of people who died of heroin overdose than in the hair of people who were still using, which it reads as suggesting a period of lower than normal use, and so lost tolerance, before death, and says that information on the rate of loss of tolerance for euphoric, analgesic and respiratory effects is sparse. It adds that the loss is likely to be non-uniform between effects and may be quite rapid, since receptor changes can take place in minutes or hours.

tasks.locator: Tolerance, paragraph beginning 'Tolerance to respiratory depression in animals'
tasks.extracted: As described by the review: tolerance to breathing depression in animals is relatively slow and incomplete compared with other opioid effects, and there is some evidence of this in people: two studies of people on methadone maintenance (Marks and Goldring, 1973; Santiago and colleagues, 1977) showed that tolerance to the breathing-depressing effect of methadone was incomplete; the review concludes that even people who have used opioids for a long time are at significant risk of breathing depression.

tasks.locator: Main text, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The review states that overdose risk appears to be increased after periods of relative abstinence, for example following incarceration or detoxification, and puts this down to lowered tolerance, citing White and Irvine; it gives no figures. White and Irvine write of a period of abstinence and of naltrexone treatment, not of incarceration or detoxification.

tasks.locator: Main text, 3rd paragraph (p. 1061, left column)
tasks.extracted: The review says that people who have stopped or are cutting down on heroin may drink more, and that low or falling tolerance may be the underlying problem in the link between alcohol and fatal overdose rather than a direct effect of alcohol, citing White and Irvine; lost tolerance is offered as an alternative explanation, with no data.

tasks.locator: Main text, last paragraph (starts p. 1061)
tasks.extracted: The review lists as an unanswered question to what extent and for how long opiate substitution drugs give tolerance to the breathing depression of heroin, that is, for how long patients are protected if they relapse or take heroin on top of a prescription.
